items.title: In a first, US set to stay away from UN review of its human rights record
items.summary: The United States is set Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago. The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council , accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn’t uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council’s mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe. The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. items.summary: The Madras High Court has directed the Tamil Nadu government to examine the need for establishing additional special courts to try corruption cases after taking note of the pendency of cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act across the State [A Shahul Hameed v. State of Tamil Nadu and Others]. Justice B Pugalendhi of the Madurai Bench observed that corruption cases could not be treated as an additional responsibility of principal district and sessions judges, particularly when the law contemplated their expeditious disposal. " The pendency of 2,423 cases throughout the State, as on 30.06.2026, cannot be viewed as an ordinary workload to be dealt with as an additional responsibility by the Principal District and Sessions Judges ," the Court said. The Court noted that exclusive special courts under the Prevention of Corruption Act were functioning in only eight districts of Tamil Nadu. In the remaining 30 districts, corruption cases were being heard by principal district and sessions judges alongside their regular judicial and administrative responsibilities. items.title: Five days for some, five years for others: What the Collegium's own record says
items.summary: Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul's memoir, entitled Without Fear or Favour, has started a debate. The former judge said that ex-Chief Justice of India DY Chandrachud was too deferential to the government on appointments . He recalled a Collegium meeting where, he says, the Chief Justice took him aside and wondered whether to phone the government to check its view on a name. Chandrachud has responded that he has not read the book. He says the meetings were respectful, that Kaul never recorded a dissent and that the government has a legitimate role in appointments. We will never see the minutes of that meeting. But we can look at something else: the dates. Every Collegium recommendation has a date. So does every government notification. If names are being settled with the government before the Collegium meets, the government has little reason to sit on them afterwards and the gap between the two dates should shrink. items.title: With or without authority? The email controversy at Bombay High Court [Watch Video]
items.summary: The Bombay High Court on October 29 quashed an administrative directive that froze trustee appointments to the Shree Saptashrungi Niwasini Devi Trust in Nashik, Maharashtra A division bench comprising Justices GS Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale ruled that District Judge Anju Shende, former Special Officer to then-Chief Justice Shree Chandrashekhar, acted with gross impropriety by issuing an administrative email that halted the lawful selection process. The Court rejected Shende’s defense that she had merely relayed oral orders passed by the Chief Justice. It held that an unverified email cannot usurp judicial authority or stall statutory proceedings without the written approval of the judge. Justices GS Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale In this freewheeling chat, Bar and Bench's Neha Joshi and Mural Krishnan discuss what triggered the controversy, who sent the email, what the officer said to the Court and what the Court eventually held. [Watch the discussion on YouTube]

items.title: Possibility of crime no ground to restrict operating hours of licensed bars: Kerala High Court
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Tuesday held that the Police cannot impose restrictions on the timings of DJ parties conducted by establishments with appropriate liquor licences (FL-3 permits) that allow their operation during extended hours [ Mahadevan v State of Kerala & ors ]. Justice Murali Purushothaman opined that the mere possibility of criminal activities is no ground to impose restrictions on the operation of such facilities. " Mere possibility of criminal activities cannot, by itself, constitute sufficient justification for imposing restrictions under the Kerala Police Act on the extended operating hours of FL3 hotels permitted under the Foreign Liquor Amendment Rules," the Court said. The Court held that while the Police have a responsibility to curb crime, it cannot restrict the activities of licenced bars by merely citing suspicions of criminal activities like drug use at such premises, unless rules restricting such bar timings are put in place by the State. items.title: Examining allegations of separatism against Waris Punjab De: ECI to Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Election Commission of India (ECI) told the Delhi High Court that it received a “grave and serious” objection to registering ‘Waris Punjab De’ as a political party, stating that it could adversely affect the “sovereignty and integrity of India." Waris Punjab, meaning ‘Heirs of Punjab’, was founded by actor-activist Deep Sidhu in 2021. Jailed pro-Khalistan Member of Parliament (MP) Amritpal Singh now heads it. The organisation plans to contest the Punjab Assembly elections due in early 2027. The ECI said that on July 9, 2026, it received a “very sensitive input” alleging that Waris Punjab De is “rooted in separatism”, was founded by individuals detained under the National Security Act (NSA) and “poses grave concerns regarding its allegiance to sovereignty and integrity of India”. It said that while the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) of Punjab gave a positive verification report about the organisation on April 27, 2026, the objection about its separatist roots was received in July 2026, and the CEO was then instructed to conduct a "comprehensive background inquiry." Reflecting on the coalition’s losses in a few places, including Anantapur and tribal districts such as Alluri Sitharama Raju, Chandrababu Naidu said: “I have said in the past that forcible conversions have happened.
